record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: For biological materials that are amorphous, active, and often glassy, are the concepts used for passive glassy physics—such as jammed and unjammed states, yielding, ductility, and brittleness—relevant for biological function, and how should active forces, feedback, local protein regulation, mechanotransduction, and biological time and length scales be incorporated into such approaches?

evidence.quote: These systems are de facto amorphous, hence it is relevant to ask whether the usual glassy physics known for passive systems may be relevant for biological functions.

However, the additional complexity of biological systems, which include internal active forces that interact with external forces, including feedback, introduces new challenges (see Fig. 7). This then requires incorporating these new microscopic mechanisms, such as local protein concentration and regulation through active transport inside the cell or mechanotransduction pathways 228 into our approaches, which impose different time scales and length scales.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider biological materials (such as living tissues, cytoskeletal networks, and intracellular environments) that are simultaneously amorphous (lacking long-range order), active (driven out of equilibrium by internal energy-consuming processes such as molecular motors and protein turnover), and often glassy (exhibiting slow relaxation, dynamical heterogeneity, and arrested dynamics). For passive amorphous solids, a well-developed theoretical framework describes jammed versus unjammed states, yielding transitions, and the distinction between ductile and brittle mechanical responses under deformation.

Address the following:

(a) Determine to what extent the passive-glass notions of jamming/unjamming, yielding, ductility, and brittleness remain meaningful descriptors of the mechanical and dynamical behavior of active amorphous biological materials, and identify which biological functions (e.g., tissue morphogenesis, wound healing, cell migration, mechanical stability of cells) are governed by these notions.

(b) Formulate a theoretical/modeling framework that extends the passive-glass description by incorporating (i) internal active forces and their feedback with externally applied forces, (ii) local regulation of protein concentration and active intracellular transport, (iii) mechanotransduction pathways, and (iv) the distinct biological time scales and length scales associated with these mechanisms. Specify how these ingredients modify the phase diagram, the yielding criterion, and the ductile-to-brittle transition in such systems.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broad conceptual research question at the interface of soft matter physics and biology. It is an actively investigated area (active glasses, tissue mechanics, jamming in epithelia) with no comprehensive resolution; current literature provides only partial results for specific systems (e.g., jamming transitions in confluent tissues, active glass simulations).

status_evidence.title: Glassy dynamics in models of confluent tissue with mitosis and apoptosis
status_evidence.snippet: Active glassy behavior in biological tissues is an open area of research.
status_evidence.claim: Question of how active processes modify glassy/jamming behavior in tissues remains under active investigation.
